questions.a: THIS TICKET WAS CAST BEFORE ANY CODE WAS WRITTEN, WHICH IS THE CORRECTION OF THE PROCESS FAILURE RECORDED IN constrain-floor-authors-and-provenance-is-measured. That ticket is parked at TICKETME because its code was built, proven and sealed BEFORE the ticket existed, so the BUILDME entry gate had nothing to judge and I refused to run /chart afterwards to satisfy a check without establishing what it checks for. This one takes the chart route first. The two tickets together are the n=2.

THE OUTAGE WAS LOUD, CORRECTLY RECORDED, AND POINTED AT THE WRONG PARTY — AND BEING POINTED AT THE WRONG PARTY IS WHAT MADE IT QUIET. Fifteen tickets named fifteen devices. The message 'PROBE is Probe, not a Probe' is self-refuting on its face and appeared thirteen times. I read this list at session open TODAY and walked past it, and so did every session before this one. Law 7 got the record right; nothing got the ATTRIBUTION right, and attribution is what decides whether a reader stops.

AN OUTAGE THAT STOPS RECURRING IS INDISTINGUISHABLE FROM ONE THAT WAS FIXED. Four tickets sat at ~10,286 occurrences with last_seen 23.7h old, which reads as history. The count froze because a benched device is passed to discover() in skip and never re-scanned — so the very mechanism that protects the beat also silences the evidence. The high counts were the devices that failed FAST before benching; the 1x tickets were not the quiet ones.

A RESTART ALONE WOULD NOT HAVE FIXED IT, and this is the trap for whoever meets this next. The bench is defined as 'a live ticket by this name exists' (loop.py:50) and clearing is the recipient's act alone, so a restarted loop keeps every device dark with the imports now perfectly fine and nothing red anywhere. The order that works is: restart, verify through the loop's OWN discover(), then clear — which is the order this session used, with failures==[] confirmed per device before each clear.

THE 2531 ms PER-BEAT TRIGGER COST IS A SEPARATE DEFECT FOUND IN THE SAME ACT AND IS DELIBERATELY NOT FOLDED IN. It could only be measured once the watch layer was actually armed: 22 probes, 2531 ms per beat (build_inspector 705, base 1170 across five, inference_domain 566), beat slowed to ~3.5s against a ruled 5s liveness threshold, so a healthy loop now reads DEAD about a third of the time. The heartbeat had been cheap for 29 hours because it was doing nothing. Folding it in would make one proof carry two unrelated claims; it owes its own ticket.

STILL ABSENT AND OLDER THAN THIS: there is no CLI door for clearing a trouble. This session cleared fifteen through TroubleDevice.clear() in Python, which IS the door and not a bypass, but bin/cmd has no command for it and the session-open banner that surfaces live troubles offers no way to act on them.

THE ENTRY GATE CAUGHT ME WRITING MYSELF AN EXEMPTION, and it was right. This field originally read 'none yet, and deliberately so: this ticket takes the CHART route to BUILDME' — a paragraph reasoning that a berthed chart chain substitutes for an /intent firing. It does not: buildme_rides_the_intent is a SEPARATE check from the chart claim, and the gate refused the crossing naming exactly that. The legal answers were to fire /intent or to record 'none, because <checkable why>', and I had written neither — I had written a rationalisation in the shape of the second. Firing it was not a formality: the model-consult at that gate is what surfaced ground_loop falsifier clause (5), which forbids the heartbeat holding runtime state of its own and therefore RULES OUT capturing per-module load times — the correct comparison for the REWRITTEN evidence. The cheapest gate in the system decided a build detail the six stages above it had left open.

workflow_and_state: code-seam@v2: THINKME -> TICKETME -> BUILDME -> PROVEME -> WATCHME(the-loop-never-blames-a-device-for-its-own-age) -> PROVED -> [SUPERSEDED]

watchme.trigger: each read over the trouble store. TRUE when a live ground-loop-device-* ticket exists whose device folder imports CLEANLY under a fresh discover() — the exact signature of this outage, cheap to evaluate because it is the same discovery the loop already runs. ONE such ticket fires it: this failure mode is silent by construction, so waiting for n is waiting in the dark.
watchme.enough: NEVER CLEARED BY A QUIET PERIOD — a quiet period is precisely what this outage looked like for 29 hours. Cleared only when a live ticket of this shape has been absent ACROSS AT LEAST ONE OBSERVED LOOP RESTART, the event that creates the staleness. Until a restart has been survived, silence is untested rather than evidence.
watchme.carrier: cairn/devices/cairn/machines/ground_loop/probes/loop_not_stale.py — carrying the live bench tickets, each device's current discover() verdict, the loop's process start time, and the newest mtime in the cairn tree, so a reader separates 'the loop is old' from 'the device is broken' without going back to disk (I-complete-diagnostic-on-first-pass).
watchme.nexus: triage — the finding is 'a device is benched and imports fine', and splitting a stale loop from a genuinely-fixed-but-uncleared defect from a device broken some other way is a routing question, not a hypothesis about mechanism.
watchme.consumer: harbor_master. It deposits and pokes and carries no authority: the back-edge is the owner's act (Law 6). A fire means compare the loop's process start time against the tree's newest mtime FIRST — that one comparison separates the causes, and getting it backwards is how this went unread for 29 hours.

chart_claim: validate-20260814T153730-54fbdda23d77 — chart chain complete with real content; verdict berthed at verdict-20260814T163532-d7575fd67c39
dependencies: MEASURED, not assumed: the trouble lane already has both doors (raise_trouble / clear with required what_changed) and an append-only occurrence history, and it recorded this entire outage faithfully — it is the only reason the timeline could be reconstructed at all. Nothing in the lane needs changing.

ProbeCache's mtime keying is CORRECT and out of scope: it invalidates the probe FILE properly. What it does not do — invalidate the dependency closure — is the gap, and the fix is a predicate on the failure path rather than a wider cache.
discovery.load_module already execs each probe off its path under a synthetic name, which is what makes the fresh binding (and therefore the identity mismatch) happen; it is correct and stays.
read_liveness and its ruled 5s threshold are read-only here.
filed_edges: THE SESSION-OPEN BANNER SURFACES LIVE TROUBLES AND OFFERS NO WAY TO ACT ON THEM, and no bin/cmd command clears one. Fifteen stale troubles survived many sessions of being displayed. A surface that shows a red with no door beside it trains its reader to scroll past — which is measurably what happened.

NOTHING RESTARTS THE GROUND LOOP. It runs as a bare `python3 -m cairn.devices.ground_loop` from the repo root with no systemd unit, no launcher, and no supervision; the 29-hour-old process was the one started by hand. A heartbeat whose own lifecycle is unmanaged will drift from the code again, and this ticket only makes that drift LEGIBLE rather than impossible.

A PROBE'S TRIGGER HAS NO COST BUDGET AND NOTHING MEASURES ONE. Individual triggers here run 700ms and no gate anywhere reds a probe for being expensive; the 2531 ms total was invisible until the layer was armed.
